summary: For ages 9–11: how climate change affects the poles, centred on the hardest idea — positive feedback LOOPS. Learners trace two self-reinforcing cycles (ice-albedo and permafrost-carbon), distinguish floating sea ice (melting barely changes sea level) from land ice sheets (melting raises sea level), and connect these to polar amplification (the Arctic is warming much faster than the global average; warming across Antarctica is more uneven). The headline interactive proposal has learners operate a climate dashboard so the self-feeding nature of a loop becomes causal and visible; supporting activities build the loop via ordering/sorting, a scientist-style spoken explanation, and evidence reading from real sea-ice data. Framing stays evidence-based and cause-and-effect, with agency (human emissions and choices affect the pace) rather than doom.
misconceptions: Melting Arctic sea ice raises sea level — floating ice melting barely changes it; land ice (Greenland/Antarctica) is what raises seas
The poles warm at the same rate as everywhere else — they warm faster (polar amplification)
A feedback loop is a single effect — it is a self-reinforcing cycle where the output feeds back to grow the cause
Permafrost is just frozen soil with no climate role — thawing it releases methane/CO2 that add further warming
It's too late / nothing affects it — the pace depends on human greenhouse-gas emissions and choices

activities.title: Run the polar climate dashboard (operate the feedback loop)
steps: Nudge a temperature control up one notch and watch a patch of bright sea ice melt into dark open ocean
Watch an albedo (reflectiveness) meter drop and an 'absorbed sunlight' reading rise as bright ice becomes dark water

Stop touching the control and observe that the exposed dark water keeps absorbing extra heat and melts some more ice — an arrow curls back to show melt causing more melt, so the total change ends up bigger than your single nudge alone would cause
Open a second panel: thaw permafrost, watch methane/CO2 puff out, push the temperature up, and thaw still more permafrost
Compare two gauges: melting the FLOATING sea ice barely moves the sea-level bar, but tipping meltwater off the Greenland LAND ice sheet clearly raises it
Pull a 'cut emissions' lever and see every loop slow down
activities.insight: A positive feedback loop is a self-reinforcing cycle: the output (melted ice / released methane) feeds back to strengthen its own cause, so a warming push leads to more warming and melting than it would on its own. Only land ice adds significant water to the sea; floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water, so its melting barely changes sea level.

activities.title: Build the loop from parts (label and order the cycle)
steps: Lay out the stages of the ice-albedo loop — bright ice reflects sunlight; ice melts; dark ocean is exposed; more heat is absorbed; warming increases — and arrange them into a closed circle rather than a straight line
Draw the return arrow from 'warming increases' back to 'ice melts' to show the cycle feeds itself
Repeat for the permafrost-carbon loop: thaw → methane/CO2 released → more warming → more thaw
Sort statements into 'raises sea level' (land-ice melt) and 'barely changes sea level' (floating sea-ice melt)
activities.insight: Assembling the cycle shows that the final step loops back to the first, which is what distinguishes a feedback loop from a one-off change.

activities.title: Explain it like a climate scientist
steps: In your own words, explain to a listener why Arctic sea ice loss is bigger than warming alone would cause — say what happens AND why the loop makes the change bigger
Add permafrost thaw as a second reinforcing loop in your explanation
Answer a probing follow-up: 'Is there anything that would make it slow down on its own, or does the loop only push one way?'
Answer: 'What if the ocean under the ice had somehow stayed white — would the melting still speed up?' and justify your answer
activities.insight: Producing a spoken cause-and-effect explanation forces the learner to close the causal circle and transfer the loop idea to a new case, rather than listing facts.

activities.title: Read the evidence: sea-ice extent over time
steps: Study an Arctic September sea-ice extent graph covering the satellite record (since 1979) and describe the trend in your own words
State roughly how fast the September minimum is falling per decade and explain how you read it from the graph
Answer: 'What's your evidence that the ice is really shrinking, not just moving around from year to year?'
activities.insight: The downward trend is evidenced by measured data, not asserted; a long record distinguishes a real decline from year-to-year wobble.

checkQuestion: In summer the sea ice near the North Pole melts, showing dark ocean underneath. The next summer, even more ice melts than the year before. Why does the melting speed up year after year instead of staying the same? Tell me what's happening, and then tell me WHY that makes it get faster.
checkAnswer: Bright white ice reflects most of the Sun's energy back to space; dark ocean absorbs it. When ice melts it uncovers dark water, which warms up and absorbs more heat, which melts more ice, which uncovers more dark water — a self-reinforcing feedback loop, so the warming and melting accelerate rather than staying steady. (Arctic September sea-ice is declining about 12% per decade.)
